errors.english: the cowherd's mother will come to know through unrest
errors.why: ཞི་བ is the name of the cowherd's mother (Śānti), the same Śānti whose hand throws the curd pot in the gloss; it is not 'unrest'.

fix.find: the cowherd's mother will come to know through unrest
fix.replace: the cowherd's mother Śānti will come to know

errors.why: ཚང here is 'nest', glossed on the next side as a dwelling (གནས་ཡིན་ནོ), not 'complete'.

note: A lemma-by-lemma Vinaya glossary that is mostly sound, but it turns the proper name Śānti into 'unrest'.
A faithful rendering of the general and specific, indirect and direct characteristics of the Truths.

errors.english: a momentary thing produces an effect that arises in a single moment
errors.why: 'Occurring in a single moment' (ekakṣaṇabhāvin) qualifies the producing thing, not the effect.

note: A sound translation of the momentariness argument, with one qualifier attached to the wrong noun.

errors.english: If the fire on the crown of Indra's head [note: a reference to a specific type of plant or phenomenon traditionally contrasted with true fire]
errors.why: Śakramūrdhan ('Indra's head') is the stock Pramāṇa example of an anthill whose vapour looks like smoke; the verse says 'if the anthill had the nature of fire, it would be fire itself', and the note is wrong.

fix.find: If the fire on the crown of Indra's head [note: a reference to a specific type of plant or phenomenon traditionally contrasted with true fire]
fix.replace: If the anthill (śakramūrdhan, 'Indra's head') [note: an anthill, whose rising vapour resembles smoke]

errors.english: from dissimilar types such as slightly heavy [note: substances]
errors.why: ལྕི་བ here is cow-dung, the classic dissimilar cause from which a lotus-type plant is said to grow; it does not mean 'heavy'.

fix.find: from dissimilar types such as slightly heavy [note: substances]
fix.replace: from dissimilar types such as cow-dung

errors.english: produce the effect without a sequence
errors.why: རྣམ་གྲངས་མེད་པར means 'not alternatively', i.e. jointly rather than each one separately; it is not about sequence.

note: The argument structure is right, but the anthill and cow-dung examples are both misread.

errors.english: much like a person who is the object of desire
errors.why: མངོན་པར་འདོད་པ here is 'accepted/intended' (abhimata): the person under discussion in the dream example, not a desired person.

errors.english: That is not the nature of reality itself.
errors.why: The root line says that this is not known as it really is (by all who do not see the supreme), which the commentary takes up with 'by whom?'; it is not a claim about the nature of reality.

note: A good rendering of the elephant-gaze passage, with two misreadings in its opening lines.

errors.english: Being blue, he is the son of that father, because of being it, like the other appearing.
errors.why: This is the stock pseudo-reason 'he is dark, because he is that father's son, like the other sons seen'; the English swaps the thesis and the reason.

fix.find: Being blue, he is the son of that father, because of being it, like the other appearing.
fix.replace: He is dark, because he is that father's son, like the other [sons] that are seen.

errors.english: For example, even if someone has three sons,
errors.why: The whole side is verse (seven-syllable pādas) and is run together as one block of prose, which blurs the boundaries between the arguments.

note: A very literal, hard-to-follow prose rendering of verse on anyathānupapatti, with one example inverted.

errors.english: the object of cognition and the negation of that object are designated as existing because they are present, while their reversal is the non-existence of non-perception
errors.why: The Tibetan says that cognition and its object are, by designation, the existence of the thing to be negated, and that their absence is non-perception, i.e. non-existence; 'negation of that object' and 'non-existence of non-perception' are wrong.

fix.find: the object of cognition and the negation of that object are designated as existing because they are present, while their reversal is the non-existence of non-perception
fix.replace: cognition and its object are, by designation, the existence of the thing to be negated, while their absence is non-perception, that is, non-existence

errors.english: by using signs that are not incompatible with the body or the mind
errors.why: The Mīmāṃsakas' reasons are having a body, having an intellect and the like, which are not incompatible with omniscience; the English inverts what is compatible with what.

fix.find: by using signs that are not incompatible with the body or the mind
fix.replace: by using reasons such as having a body or an intellect, which are not incompatible with omniscience and the like

errors.english: it is affected by the transformative power of the object or the sense faculties
errors.why: The object or the faculty is the thing affected by (an external) adhiṣṭhāna; the power does not belong to them.

errors.english: other qualifying characteristics such as the dewlap will be explained after the characteristics of the cow are reversed
errors.why: The dewlap and so on are the cow's marks (nimitta) whose absence is meant; the 'other' is the marked thing (nimittin), so the two are conflated.

note: The non-perception passage is garbled at key points, though the rest of the logic is followed.

span_why: It opens with the husband's reply ('Good lady, what you say is not wrong'), the bath and the new clothes, all of which are on the previous side.
note: A faithful narrative translation of the Upananda episode, prefixed by material from the previous side.

errors.why: They act toward an object capable of arthakriyā (causal efficacy); they are not 'engaging in purposeful action'.

note: A solid rendering of the apoha discussion of conceptual cognition and conventional users.

errors.english: This is because all is understood through the function of the eye.
errors.why: This is an unwanted consequence ('for then everything would be known by the operation of the eye'), and the English states it as a fact.

errors.english: Therefore, one object possesses many aspects.
errors.why: The verse says that a single cognition has many objects (the point being that non-conceptual cognition grasps many at once), not that one object has many aspects.

note: A generally accurate account of the citra-cognition debate; the closing verse and one prasaṅga are misread.
